answer: A boolean array/list, e.g. matrix[[True, False]], is advanced indexing: it's treated as a mask over axis 0, so you get row 0. A bare Python bool used as its own element inside an index tuple works differently: each scalar bool is a 0-d boolean index that does NOT consume an existing axis. Instead it inserts a new axis, sized 1 if True (like a conditional np.newaxis, keeping that slice) or sized 0 if False (making that axis empty). So matrix[True, False] inserts a size-1 axis then a size-0 axis, giving shape (1,0,2,2) - empty. matrix[True, True] inserts two size-1 axes, shape (1,1,2,2), which still holds the whole matrix (not empty). matrix[True, True, False] inserts three such axes (sizes 1,1,0) the same way, regardless of matrix only having 2 real dimensions, because scalar bools never index into existing dimensions - they only prepend new axes based on truthiness, and don't count toward "too many indices" errors. Rule of thumb: use an array/list of bools to mask an axis; scalar bools in a tuple do newaxis-style insertion instead.

"Tracked actor is not managed" is an internal Ray Tune actor-bookkeeping error, and it's usually a symptom, not the root cause - it means a trial's actor died or errored before Tune could register/track it properly. Check the full trial error log (~/ray_results/.../error.txt) for the real underlying exception. Likely causes here: (1) ray.tune.integration.pytorch_lightning.TuneReportCheckpointCallback is the old, largely unmaintained integration path for recent Ray/Lightning versions - switch to ray.train.lightning.RayTrainReportCallback with ray.train.lightning.prepare_trainer; (2) a version mismatch between ray, pytorch-lightning, and optuna; (3) an exception thrown inside train_model or the search space itself (e.g. tune.sample_from's lambda uses np - confirm numpy is actually imported in that module) that crashes the trial immediately. Try running train_model directly (no Tuner) with one fixed config first to confirm it works standalone, then reintroduce Tune/Optuna with pinned, mutually-compatible package versions.

No library is guaranteed to work on every host; the failures you're seeing on Render usually come from either missing system binaries (pyttsx3 needs espeak/espeak-ng installed at the OS level, which Render's default Python environment doesn't include) or blocked/rate-limited outbound calls (gTTS and edge-tts both hit external web endpoints, which can fail or throttle on shared hosting). For something genuinely self-contained, Piper TTS is a real offline neural engine - but you must bundle the .onnx voice model files inside your deployment image (not fetch them at runtime) and install the piper binary as a build step, so nothing needs network access when generating speech. Write raw audio to WAV, then convert to mp3 with pydub + ffmpeg (add ffmpeg as a system package too). If your Render plan supports a Dockerfile-based service rather than the native buildpack, use that - it gives you control to apt-get install espeak-ng/ffmpeg and vendor piper's model files, which is the actual fix, not a different pip package.

Stay in Polars/Arrow instead of pulling to Python lists first. Concatenate the two Series and explode+unique natively:

unique_vals = (
    pl.concat([df.get_column("a"), df.get_column("b")])
    .explode()
    .unique()
)

or across both columns via concat_list:

df.select(pl.concat_list(["a", "b"]).alias("x")).select(pl.col("x").explode().unique())

Both run entirely in Rust over the Series, avoiding the Python-level to_list() + set comprehension, which forces full materialization into Python objects plus a Python-level loop - that's the actual slow part, not Polars. .explode() flattens the list columns and .unique() dedups; only call .to_list() at the very end if you need a plain Python list.

This is almost always about where the output is rendered, not the ANSI codes. VS Code's integrated terminal supports 24-bit truecolor ANSI escapes fine, but the Debug Console, the Jupyter/interactive output panel, and some "Output" tabs don't render ANSI color - they show raw escape sequences or strip them, which looks like missing/garbled color. Make sure you run the script via the terminal-based runner (the Run Python File button, or Ctrl+F5 "Run Without Debugging", which opens a real integrated terminal), not by hitting the debug (bug icon) button, which sends output to the Debug Console instead. Also confirm you're not running it inside a Jupyter cell/interactive window, which has the same limitation. If it's still wrong in the actual integrated terminal, check the terminal profile isn't a legacy cmd.exe session with virtual terminal processing disabled - use the default PowerShell or Windows Terminal profile.

Simplest robust check: don't parse stat at all - compare the inode of the open /proc/<pid> directory file descriptors. Each time the kernel reuses a pid number for a new process, /proc/<pid> is backed by a fresh, distinct inode; the old one disappears when the original process exits. So:

st1 = os.fstat(pid_dir_fd1)
st2 = os.fstat(pid_dir_fd2)
same_process = st1.st_ino == st2.st_ino and st1.st_dev == st2.st_dev

That's cheaper than reading and parsing stat's starttime field and relies on the same underlying guarantee. Your starttime approach is also correct in principle - (pid, starttime) is the canonical unique process identity per proc(5) - just double check your field parsing is robust (comm can contain spaces/parens, but indexing from the ')' as you did is the standard-safe way). pidfd (os.pidfd_open, Linux 5.3+) is the newer race-free primitive, but it's mainly for detecting exit via poll/select, not for tagging cached per-process data - inode or starttime comparison is simpler for your use case.

squarify only lays out one flat level, so build the leaf-level layout yourself and color by the parent group instead of nesting boxes. Sort by group then value, run squarify on the leaf sizes only, and color each rectangle by its parent (city), with a manual legend instead of group labels:

import squarify, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
d = df.sort_values(["city","sales"], ascending=[True,False])
norm = squarify.normalize_sizes(d["sales"], 100, 100)
rects = squarify.squarify(norm, 0, 0, 100, 100)
colors = {c: plt.cm.tab10(i) for i,c in enumerate(d["city"].unique())}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for r,(_,row) in zip(rects, d.iterrows()):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((r["x"],r["y"]), r["dx"], r["dy"], color=colors[row["city"]], ec="white"))
    ax.text(r["x"]+r["dx"]/2, r["y"]+r["dy"]/2, row["product"], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,100); ax.set_ylim(0,100); ax.axis("off")
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=v,label=k) for k,v in colors.items()], bbox_to_anchor=(1,1))

This yields only leaf rectangles, colored/legended by top-level group - Plotly's px.treemap can't do this since it always draws parent boxes too.

multiprocessing forks (or spawns + pickles) each worker, so every process gets its own private copy of a - writes never propagate back to the parent, which is exactly what you're seeing with both joblib and Pool.starmap. To actually share and mutate memory across processes you need real shared memory, not a copied argument:

from multiprocessing import Process, shared_memory
import numpy as np
shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=10)
a = np.ndarray((10,), dtype=np.uint8, buffer=shm.buf)

def Test(i, shm_name, length):
    ex = shared_memory.SharedMemory(name=shm_name)
    arr = np.ndarray((length,), dtype=np.uint8, buffer=ex.buf)
    arr[i % 2::2] = 2 if i % 2 == 0 else 1
    ex.close()

procs = [Process(target=Test, args=(i, shm.name, 10)) for i in range(2)]
[p.start() for p in procs]; [p.join() for p in procs]

multiprocessing.Array/RawArray works similarly for simpler ctypes cases. Alternatively, since numpy releases the GIL during array operations, just use threads (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor) - they share memory natively, no serialization needed, and the GIL won't bottleneck this kind of workload.

Requesting a DEM per 256x256 patch is almost certainly what's slow - each py3dep call is a separate network round trip, and with 122k patches that per-request overhead dominates, not the actual data volume. Since your patches are grouped into only 169 ROIs, request the DEM once per ROI (covering the full bounding box of all patches in that ROI, padded a bit) instead of once per patch - about 169 requests instead of 122k. Then crop each patch's DEM locally and fast with rasterio (rasterio.windows.from_bounds or rasterio.mask) against the single downloaded ROI raster, no further network calls needed, and reuse it across every patch that shares that ROI. If ROI-level 3DEP queries are still slow, consider a bulk source built for large-area downloads instead of many small point queries - e.g. AWS's public Terrain Tiles / Copernicus GLO-30 on registry.opendata.aws, or OpenTopography's bulk API.

Standard pattern: don't autogenerate against each live tenant DB. Keep one reference/"template" database - it needn't be public-facing, an ephemeral sqlite or a private dev Postgres you control is fine - that always reflects the current head of your migration history, and run alembic revision --autogenerate against that one. At deploy time, loop over tenants and call alembic upgrade head (applying the already-authored migration script) against each tenant's connection string - not autogenerate - so there's no per-tenant schema comparison at all. Your "Target database is not up to date" error happens because autogenerate refuses to diff a DB whose alembic_version isn't already stamped at the latest known revision; that check becomes irrelevant once you separate "author migrations against one reference DB" from "apply migrations to N tenant DBs". In env.py, parametrize the target connection (e.g. via -x tenant=<id> or an env var) so the same generated scripts run unmodified across all tenants.

A single nested comprehension does this directly:

mapped = [(r, c) for r, sub in zip(rows, cols) for c in sub]

zip(rows, cols) pairs each row value with its corresponding sub-list; the inner for c in sub then unpacks that sub-list into individual tuples (r, c), one per element - exactly the (row[i], cols[i][j]) pattern you want, and it naturally handles cols sub-lists of different lengths without any extra bookkeeping.

With only a coarse camera_distance and no real intrinsics/calibration, plain rotation-matrix alignment will drift. Two likely culprits: (1) rotating about the array's geometric center instead of the true physical turntable axis - you need to translate points so the rotation axis sits at the origin, rotate by the known per-shot angle, then translate back; (2) treating pixel (x,y) grid positions as metric coordinates without passing them through the camera's actual intrinsics/projection model first, which distorts the point cloud before rotation is even applied. Rather than hand-rolling this, convert each depth map to a point cloud with correct intrinsics (e.g. Open3D's create_from_depth_image), apply your known turntable rotation as an initial guess, then refine with ICP (open3d.pipelines.registration.registration_icp) to correct residual calibration/axis error before merging. Open3D also provides voxel downsampling and outlier removal to clean up overlap once merged. Rotation matrices aren't wrong in principle, just insufficient alone without exact calibration - ICP-based registration is the standard fix for real, non-simulated data like this.

This is documented np.vectorize behavior: without otypes specified, it runs your function once on the first element as a "trial call" purely to determine the output dtype (it needs to know what dtype to allocate for the result array), then runs the real vectorized loop over every element - including that same first element again. So a length-1 input produces 2 calls total (1 probe + 1 real), and length-n produces n+1, with only the first element called twice. Avoid the extra call by telling vectorize the output type(s) up front, which skips the dtype-probing step entirely:

np.vectorize(f, otypes=[object])(["input"])

(use whatever dtype matches your actual return type, e.g. otypes=[float] for numeric output). With otypes given, f is called exactly once per input element.

From a clean binary mask, the standard PlantCV route to a length measurement is the morphology submodule: skeletonize, prune spurious spurs, then measure path length along the skeleton (exact argument names shift a bit by PlantCV version, but the pipeline is stable):

skel = pcv.morphology.skeletonize(mask=cleaned_mask)
pruned, seg_img, edge_objects = pcv.morphology.prune(skel_img=skel, size=N, mask=cleaned_mask)
seg_img2, labeled = pcv.morphology.segment_skeleton(skel_img=pruned, mask=cleaned_mask)
pcv.morphology.segment_path_length(segmented_img=seg_img2, objects=labeled, label="root")

segment_path_length stores each segment's pixel length in pcv.outputs.observations; sum the segments for total root length if it's one unbranched root, or keep them separate for the branched image. Tune the prune size threshold visually (debug="plot") so it removes fill() leftovers without cutting real root tips. For real-world units instead of pixels, include a reference object of known size in-frame and convert via that pixel-to-cm ratio.

Extracting the zip only puts files on disk; QGIS won't pick up a new plugin until it's actually loaded and started in the running session. After extraction, call:

import qgis.utils
qgis.utils.loadPlugin(plugin_name)
qgis.utils.startPlugin(plugin_name)

loadPlugin imports the plugin module and registers it in qgis.utils.plugins/active_plugins; startPlugin calls its initGui(), which is what actually creates the toolbar button/menu entry - this is the same pair of calls the Plugin Manager itself triggers when a user installs and enables a plugin without restarting. If you also want it enabled on future normal startups (not just this session), make sure the QSettings key "PythonPlugins/<plugin_name>" ends up set to true, which startPlugin/the plugin manager flow normally handles automatically. Make sure extraction has fully finished (files written, __init__.py present with a valid classFactory) before calling loadPlugin, or the import can silently fail on that first attempt.

Rather than combining two CumulVars from your existing Duration dimension after the fact, give ride time its own dimension that resets to 0 at each pickup. Add a second dimension with the same per-arc transit (travel + service time) as Duration, then force its cumul to 0 exactly at every pickup node:

routing.solver().Add(ride_dim.CumulVar(pickup_index) == 0)

for each pickup in your pickup-delivery pairs. After that, ride_dim's cumulative value at each delivery node directly equals that passenger's ride time (pickup-to-delivery elapsed time) as a normal CumulVar - so you can use the built-in soft-bound support directly, no big-M or auxiliary max() needed:

ride_dim.SetCumulVarSoftUpperBound(delivery_index, 60, penalty_coefficient)

This "reset at node" trick is the same pattern used for things like distance-since-refueling in OR-Tools' own examples, adapted to pickup-delivery ride time. Tune penalty_coefficient to control how strongly violations are discouraged relative to your other objective terms.

One real bug first: inside the loop you reassign the name data to a plain list (data_set["values"] = data, after labels, data = list(set.keys()), list(set.values())), which shadows your outer DataFrame data - so on the next iteration for name, values in data.items() breaks, since data is now a list. Rename the inner variable (e.g. counts), and set (a builtin) too. For the actual tallying, value_counts() is already the right, vectorized tool - nothing more "efficient" is needed. What's missing is consistent ordering: value_counts() sorts by frequency, not Likert order, and silently drops response options with zero count. Define the scale explicitly and reindex instead:

order = ["Never","Occasionally","Frequently","Always"]
counts = pd.Categorical(values.dropna(), categories=order, ordered=True)
counts = pd.Series(counts).value_counts().reindex(order, fill_value=0)

That guarantees consistent bar order across charts and includes zero-count categories.
